title: Good Stress or Bad Stress?
author: Delving, Michel
summary: The author distinguishes 'good' stress (eustress), which builds long-term capacity and resilience, from 'bad' stress (distress), which erodes health and motivation, and argues that schools should teach children this distinction starting in the earliest years of formal education. The same stressor can be good or bad depending on duration, intensity, and recovery time, as illustrated by a weightlifting analogy: the same exercise is beneficial on day one and harmful by day three without recovery. The piece connects this to modern culture's tendency to design rest and recovery out of daily life via always-on work, social media, and a stigma against idleness. It concludes that children need to learn both that stress is sometimes necessary and that recovery must be interwoven with it, not treated as a reward saved for the end.
points: Eustress (good stress) leads to growth, resilience, and focus, while distress (bad stress) leads to burnout, fatigue, and exhaustion — the biological trigger is the same, but duration and recovery determine the outcome.
The same stressor (e.g., lifting weights) can be good on one day and bad the next if the body isn't given time to recover in between.
Modern culture — social media, email, remote work, and stigma against idleness — has largely designed rest and recovery out of daily life.
Teaching kids to distinguish good and bad stress should begin in the earliest years of formal schooling, not be left to chance.
The key lesson for young people is to interweave stress and recovery rather than clumping either one together for long stretches.
quotes: Good stress helps you to function at the highest level, in the way most conducive to your individuality, for as long as possible.
The main difference between good stress and bad stress comes down to duration, intensity, and your body’s ability to recover.
Eustress is short-term and manageable. Distress is long-term and overwhelming.
Western corporate culture has designed rest and recovery out of modern life. This is not okay.
It is good to sometimes feel stressed. It is good to sometimes feel relaxed. It is very good to interweave both.
Clump-hoarding either experience together for long durations of time is not healthy. Spread out the stress and spread out the relaxation.
